```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(eco)
  library(data.table)
  library(lme4)
  library(unmarked)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(plotly)
})
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
options(digits = 3)
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f")
cache <- readRDS("species_items_data/species_items.rds")
```

A community survey visits a set of sites, listens or looks for every species
on a list, and writes down which ones it found. Laid out as a table, that is
one row per site and one column per species, filled with zeros and ones. A
model for that table needs something about each site (some sites hold more
species, or a different set of them, than others) and something about each
species (some are common, some rare, some found mostly where others are not).
The multispecies occupancy model [@dorazio2005; @dorazio2006; @kery2016,
chapter 11] is such a model, with one extra layer: a zero can mean the species
is absent or that it was there and missed.

This page builds the model up from the site-by-species table, fits it to one
eco table first without and then with the detection layer, and shows what
the detection layer changes. It then fits a second, much sparser table to show
what treating species as draws from a community buys and what it cannot.

{{< include _caveat.qmd >}}

## Sites and species: the idea

Write $z_{ik} = 1$ if species $k$ occurs at site $i$. The simplest model with
something for each site and something for each species is

$$
\Pr(z_{ik} = 1) = \text{logit}^{-1}(\beta_k + \lambda_k w_i).
$$

- $w_i$ is a single number for the site that is not observed: a position on
  whatever gradient most separates the community's sites (wet to dry, young
  forest to old, disturbed to not). It is a latent variable, inferred from
  which species the site holds.
- $\beta_k$ says how common species $k$ is at a typical site ($w_i = 0$).
- $\lambda_k$ says how strongly, and in which direction, species $k$ tracks the
  gradient: a large positive $\lambda_k$ is a species found almost only at the
  high end, a negative one a species of the low end, and $\lambda_k$ near zero
  a species that does not care.

So far each species has its own free parameters. The step that makes this a
*community* model is to treat the species themselves as a sample: the
$\beta_k$ are drawn from one normal distribution with a community mean $\mu$ and
spread $\tau$,

$$
\beta_k \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_\beta, \tau^2_\beta).
$$

Species whose own data say little, the ones seen twice, are then estimated
partly from the community: their $\hat\beta_k$ is pulled toward $\mu_\beta$, more
so the less the data say. The distribution also describes the species that
were never seen at all, which is how these models estimate total species
richness [@dorazio2006]. In psychometrics the same structure, with test
questions in place of species and test-takers in place of sites, is called a
random-item response model [@deboeck2008].

The ecological model adds the survey. Species $k$ at site $i$ is surveyed on
$J_i$ visits, and a visit finds it only if it is there:

$$
y_{ijk} \mid z_{ik} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(z_{ik}\, p_k),
\qquad
\text{logit}(p_k) = \alpha_k \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_\alpha, \tau^2_\alpha).
$$

The model of sites and species is on $z$, which is never observed. What is
observed is $y$, and the probability that a survey of $J_i$ visits ever records
species $k$ is

$$
\Pr\Big(\max_j y_{ijk} = 1\Big) = \psi_{ik} \left[ 1 - (1 - p_k)^{J_i} \right],
\qquad \psi_{ik} = \text{logit}^{-1}(\beta_k + \lambda_k w_i).
$$

Fit the site-and-species model directly to the "ever detected" table and its
species parameter estimates the whole of that product: how common the species
is *and* how easy it is to find, in one number. Its site parameter absorbs how
hard the site was searched. Repeat visits are what pull the two apart, as in
the [single-species case](occupancy.html).

The standard multispecies model of @dorazio2005 sets $\lambda_k = 0$: species
have their own $\beta_k$ and $\alpha_k$ drawn from the community, and sites differ
only through covariates. Adding $\lambda_k w_i$ gives the latent-factor version
of @tobler2019, which is what puts a site parameter back into the model.
Both are fit below.

## Choosing the tables

The tables are chosen from `eco_metadata()` by rule. The model needs a site
unit, a 0/1 detection response, more than one taxon, replicate visits that can
be treated as repeats of the same state (`closure` "closed", one season, and
occasions that index time rather than observers, methods or sub-plots), enough
sites to see a pattern ($\geq 30$) and a community size where pooling matters
and a page can show every species (10 to 40). Tables that need a Redivis login
and tables whose survey set was reconstructed by rule (`survey_evidence`
"inferred") are left out.

```{r}
#| label: rule
eco_set_version(12)
cand <- as.data.table(eco_filter(unit_kind = "site", response_type = "detection",
                                 multi_species = TRUE, min_units = 30, min_occasions = 2))
cand <- merge(cand, as.data.table(eco_list_tables())[, .(table, needs_login, survey_taxa)], by = "table")
picked <- cand[closure == "closed" & n_periods == 1 & occasion_kind == "time" &
                 n_taxa >= 10 & n_taxa <= 40 & !needs_login & survey_evidence != "inferred" &
                 !grepl("_exact", table)]
picked[, .(table, n_units, n_taxa, n_occasions, survey_evidence, survey_taxa)]
stopifnot(setequal(picked$table, names(cache$fits)))
```

Of the `r nrow(cand)` multi-taxon site detection tables with at least 30 sites
and two occasions, the rule keeps two. The others fall out on the number of
seasons, the number of taxa (several community tables carry 50 to 240), or
occasions that are spatial subsamples or methods. Neither table has a
`__survey_taxa` side table, so every species was looked for on every visit and
the zeros in the table are real non-detections; a table with one would have
species-specific gaps, which `eco_to_array()` keeps as `NA` and which the
model would have to respect.

The two are very different communities, which is the point of fitting both:

- `lebeuftaylor_2026_boreal_edges_aru_comm` [@lebeuftaylor2026]: 34 bird
  species recorded within 150 m of autonomous recording units at 564 locations
  in northern Alberta, three per transect across a timber-harvest edge (150 m
  into the regenerating cut, the edge itself, 150 m into the forest), with one
  to five recording visits each. Every species was detected at 12 or more
  locations. This is the main example.
- `clipp_2024_monongahela_comm` [@clipp2024]: 35 bird and mammal species on
  129 camera traps at wildlife openings in West Virginia, one occasion per
  camera-day. White-tailed deer are detected at 114 cameras; 15 of the 35
  species at exactly one.

## The boreal table

```{r}
#| label: fetch
#| message: true
eco_info("lebeuftaylor_2026_boreal_edges_aru_comm")
d <- as.data.table(eco_fetch("lebeuftaylor_2026_boreal_edges_aru_comm"))
taxa <- as.data.table(eco_taxa("lebeuftaylor_2026_boreal_edges_aru_comm"))
```

One row per species per recording visit. `eco_to_array()` turns it into a
site $\times$ visit $\times$ species array, with `NA` wherever a location had
fewer than five visits: a missing row is a visit that did not happen, not a
miss. Permuting the dimensions gives the species $\times$ site $\times$ visit
array that spOccupancy expects.

```{r}
#| label: array
a <- eco_to_array(d)
y <- aperm(a$y, c(3, 1, 2))                       # species x site x visit
dim(y)
J <- rowSums(!is.na(y[1, , ]))                    # visits per location
table(visits = J)
# a community table without __survey_taxa: the same visits for every species
stopifnot(all(apply(y, 1, function(m) identical(is.na(m), is.na(y[1, , ])))))
ever <- apply(y, c(1, 2), max, na.rm = TRUE)      # species x site, detected on any visit
```

## Ignoring detection: sites and species on the "ever detected" table

The first fit is the site-and-species model on `ever`, with no detection
layer, as a generalised linear mixed model: a random intercept for each
location (its latent quantity) and a random intercept for each species (drawn
from the community), crossed. It is the special case of the model above in which
every species has the same loading, so every species tracks the site quantity
equally.

```{r}
#| label: naive
long <- data.table(species = rep(dimnames(y)[[1]], ncol(ever)),
                   site = rep(colnames(ever), each = nrow(ever)),
                   ever = as.vector(ever))
naive <- glmer(ever ~ 1 + (1 | site) + (1 | species), family = binomial, data = long)
VarCorr(naive)
```

The species spread (a standard deviation of
`r fmt(attr(VarCorr(naive)$species, "stddev"))` on the logit scale) dwarfs
the site spread (`r fmt(attr(VarCorr(naive)$site, "stddev"))`): which species
is asked about matters far more than where. The site intercept is easy to read
in this model, because with every species weighted equally the only thing
that moves a site up is detecting more species. Its correlation with the
count of species detected at the location is
`r fmt(cor(lme4::ranef(naive)$site[colnames(ever), 1], colSums(ever)), 3)`. It
is a detected-richness score, and detected richness depends on how often
the site was visited:

```{r}
#| label: naive-visits
site_naive <- data.table(unit = colnames(ever), visits = J, detected = colSums(ever),
                         score = lme4::ranef(naive)$site[colnames(ever), 1])
site_naive[, .(locations = .N, mean_species_detected = mean(detected), mean_score = mean(score)), keyby = visits]
```

A location recorded once scores lower than one recorded three times, not
because it holds fewer birds but because fewer were heard. Most locations here
have three visits, so the damage is limited; in a table with uneven effort it
is not.

## Separating occupancy from detection

The community occupancy model puts the species distribution on two
parameters per species, occupancy $\psi_k$ and detection $p_k$, each drawn from
its own community normal. It is fit with `spOccupancy::msPGOcc()`
[@doser2022], a Gibbs sampler that takes about two minutes on this table. The
call, from the companion script
[`species_items_compute.R`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/species_items_compute.R),
is

```{r}
#| label: ms-code
#| eval: false
library(spOccupancy)
ms <- msPGOcc(occ.formula = ~1, det.formula = ~1, data = list(y = y),
              n.samples = 6000, n.burn = 2000, n.thin = 4, n.chains = 3)
```

and the page reads its saved summaries. Both formulas are intercept-only on
purpose: every species has one $\psi_k$ and one $p_k$, nothing else, so the
comparison with the model above is like for like. (The table carries
standardised day and time of each visit, `obs_day_z` and `obs_time_z`, which a
real analysis of these birds would put on $p$.)

```{r}
#| label: ms-load
fb <- cache$fits[["lebeuftaylor_2026_boreal_edges_aru_comm"]]
fb$comm_ms[, .(parameter = param, median = med, lower = lo, upper = hi, Rhat = rhat)]
fb$conv
sp <- as.data.table(fb$species)
sp[, `:=`(psi = plogis(ms_beta), psi_lo = plogis(ms_beta_lo), psi_hi = plogis(ms_beta_hi),
          p = plogis(ms_alpha), p3 = 1 - (1 - plogis(ms_alpha))^3)]
```

All chains agree (largest $\hat R$ `r fmt(max(fb$conv$max_rhat))`). The
community's median species occupies `r fmt(plogis(fb$comm_ms[param == "mu_psi", med]))`
of locations and is detected on `r fmt(plogis(fb$comm_ms[param == "mu_p", med]))`
of visits where present. Detection varies less between species than
occupancy does, but it varies: per-visit $\hat p_k$ runs from
`r fmt(min(sp$p))` to `r fmt(max(sp$p))`, so the chance of ever recording a
species present at a three-visit location runs from `r fmt(min(sp$p3))` to
`r fmt(max(sp$p3))`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-naive-psi
#| fig-cap: "For each species, the share of locations where it was ever detected (the quantity the model without detection describes) against its occupancy under msPGOcc, with 95% credible intervals. Colour is the estimated per-visit detection probability. The gap below the diagonal is the occupied locations where the species was missed on every visit. Hover for the species."
sp[, label := sprintf("%s (%s)\ndetected at %d of %d locations\nnaive share %.2f, psi %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]\np per visit %.2f",
                      vernacularName, taxon, n_sites_detected, fb$n_sites, naive_share, psi, psi_lo, psi_hi, p)]
g <- ggplot(sp, aes(psi, naive_share, colour = p, text = label)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#c9ccc8") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = psi_lo, xmax = psi_hi), height = 0, linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#bfe3d2", high = "#0b4f33", name = "p", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 0.9), ylim = c(0, 0.9)) +
  labs(x = "Occupancy, msPGOcc", y = "Share of locations where detected")
plotly::ggplotly(g, tooltip = "text", width = 620, height = 560) |>
  plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: naive-stats
#| echo: false
sp[, gap := psi - naive_share]
worst <- sp[which.max(gap / psi)]
amro <- sp[taxon == "AMRO"]; lisp <- sp[taxon == "LISP"]
fit_check <- max(abs(sp$ms_pever - sp$naive_share))
cor_p_gap <- cor(sp$p, sp$gap / sp$psi)
```

Every species sits below the diagonal. The model without detection is not
wrong about what it estimates: the occupancy model's implied probability of
ever detecting each species, $\psi_k[1 - (1 - p_k)^{J_i}]$ averaged over the
locations' visit counts, matches the observed share to within
`r fmt(fit_check, 3)` for every species. It is wrong about what that number
means. Read as "how common is this species", it understates every species,
by a fraction that is set by detection: across species the correlation
between $\hat p_k$ and the relative shortfall is
`r fmt(cor_p_gap)`. The worst case is the `r worst$vernacularName`, detected on
`r fmt(worst$p)` of visits where present; it occupies an estimated
`r fmt(worst$psi)` of locations but was recorded at `r fmt(worst$naive_share)`.
The ordering of species changes too. American Robin and Lincoln's Sparrow
were recorded at almost the same number of locations
(`r amro$n_sites_detected` and `r lisp$n_sites_detected`), but the robin is
the harder of the two to pick up on a visit ($\hat p$ `r fmt(amro$p)` against
`r fmt(lisp$p)`), and its estimated occupancy is `r fmt(amro$psi)` against
`r fmt(lisp$psi)`.

### What the community distribution buys

Fitting each species on its own, with `unmarked::occu()` [@fiske2011], gives
the no-pooling answer: the same $\psi_k$ and $p_k$, but every species estimated
from its own detections alone.

```{r}
#| label: nopool
nopool <- rbindlist(lapply(dimnames(y)[[1]], function(k) {
  umf <- suppressMessages(eco_to_unmarked(d[taxon == k], family = "occu"))
  m <- suppressWarnings(occu(~1 ~1, umf))
  se <- tryCatch(suppressWarnings(sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))), error = function(e) c(NA, NA))
  data.table(taxon = k, np_psi = plogis(coef(m)[1]), np_psi_se = se[1])
}))
nopool[order(-np_psi)][1:4]
```

```{r}
#| label: nopool-stats
#| echo: false
sh <- merge(sp, nopool, by = "taxon")
sh[, boundary := np_psi > 0.99 | is.na(np_psi_se) | np_psi_se > 10]
ww <- sh[taxon == "WWCR"]
```

For most species the two answers agree closely. They part where a species'
own data are thin: `r sum(sh$boundary)` of the `r nrow(sh)` single-species fits
run to the boundary, $\hat\psi_k$ near 1 with no usable standard error
(missing, or above 10 on the logit scale),
because on its own a species heard at a few locations, and rarely more than
once there, is fit about as well by "present nearly everywhere, almost never
heard" as by "present at a few locations". The White-winged Crossbill is the
clearest case: `r ww$n_detections` detections at `r ww$n_sites_detected` of
`r fb$n_sites` locations. The community model does not let a species be that
unlike the others without evidence; it puts the crossbill's occupancy at
`r fmt(ww$psi)` [`r fmt(ww$psi_lo)`, `r fmt(ww$psi_hi)`], with a per-visit
detection probability near the community's.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shrink-boreal
#| fig-cap: "Occupancy with no pooling (each species fit alone with unmarked) against occupancy under the community model, boreal table. Point size is the number of locations where the species was detected; open points are single-species fits at the boundary (psi above 0.99, or a standard error missing or above 10). Hover for the species."
sh[, label2 := sprintf("%s\ndetected at %d locations\nalone: psi %.2f%s\ncommunity: psi %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]",
                       vernacularName, n_sites_detected, np_psi, ifelse(boundary, " (boundary)", ""), psi, psi_lo, psi_hi)]
g <- ggplot(sh, aes(psi, np_psi, size = n_sites_detected, text = label2)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#c9ccc8") +
  geom_point(aes(fill = boundary), shape = 21, colour = "#1e8a5a", alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#1e8a5a", `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7, guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Occupancy, community model (msPGOcc)", y = "Occupancy, each species alone (occu)")
plotly::ggplotly(g, tooltip = "text", width = 620, height = 560) |>
  plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

## Putting the site back

The community model above has no site quantity at all: two locations with
the same visits are, before seeing data, the same. The last fit adds it back,
one latent $w_i$ per location with a loading $\lambda_k$ per species on
occupancy, which is the model the first section wrote down, now with
detection underneath. `spOccupancy::lfMsPGOcc()` fits it [@tobler2019;
@doser2022]:

```{r}
#| label: lf-code
#| eval: false
lf <- lfMsPGOcc(occ.formula = ~1, det.formula = ~1, n.factors = 1,
                data = list(y = y[c(anchor, setdiff(dimnames(y)[[1]], anchor)), , ],
                            coords = matrix(0, dim(y)[2], 2)),   # required, unused without space
                n.samples = 6000, n.burn = 2000, n.thin = 4, n.chains = 3)
```

The latent variable has no units, so something has to fix its direction and
scale. spOccupancy fixes the first species' loading at 1. That species should
be one that clearly tracks whatever the gradient is: a species present
almost everywhere carries no information about $w_i$, and with the
Swainson's Thrush, the most-detected species, in first place the three chains
settled on opposite signs. The rule used here is to put first, among the
species detected at between 10% and 90% of locations, the one with the
steepest slope in a quick fit of the same model to the `ever` table
[`mirt`, @chalmers2012]. On this table that is the
`r taxa[taxon == fb$anchor, vernacularName]`, so a high $w_i$ means "more like
where `r taxa[taxon == fb$anchor, vernacularName]`s are".

```{r}
#| label: fig-loadings
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Loading of each species on the site latent variable under lfMsPGOcc, with 95% credible intervals. The anchor species' loading is fixed at 1."
ld <- copy(sp)
ld[, name := factor(vernacularName, levels = vernacularName[order(lf_lambda)])]
ggplot(ld, aes(lf_lambda, name)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#c9ccc8") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lf_lambda_lo, xmax = lf_lambda_hi), height = 0, colour = "#1e8a5a", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = "#1e8a5a", size = 2.2) +
  labs(x = expression("Loading " * lambda[k]), y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```

```{r}
#| label: lf-stats
#| echo: false
st <- as.data.table(fb$site)
pos <- st[, .(w = mean(lf_w)), keyby = .(unit_forest_type, unit_position)]
r_lam <- cor(sp$lf_lambda, sp$twopl_a)
r_vis_naive <- cor(st$visits, st$rasch_theta); r_vis_w <- cor(st$visits, st$lf_w)
hab <- summary(lm(lf_w ~ unit_position + unit_forest_type + unit_tsh_years, data = st))
```

The gradient is legible from the species alone. At the positive end are
White-throated Sparrow, Black-and-white and Mourning Warblers, Alder and Least
Flycatchers, Common Yellowthroat and American Redstart, birds of deciduous
woods and shrubby regrowth; at the negative end the White-winged Crossbill,
Yellow-rumped Warbler, the two kinglets, Hermit Thrush and Dark-eyed Junco,
birds of conifer. Ovenbird, a mature-forest ground nester that is
common on both sides, loads at zero. Most loadings are positive, so $w_i$ is also
partly a richness axis (its correlation with the posterior number of species
present at a location is `r fmt(cor(fb$site$lf_w, fb$site$ms_rich))`):
deciduous regrowth holds more of these 34 species than conifer does. The site scores agree with what the
deposit records about each location:

```{r}
#| label: fig-w
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Posterior mean of the site latent variable for each location, by forest type and position across the harvest edge (N15: 150 m into the regenerating cut; E0: the edge; P15: 150 m into the forest). Bars are group means."
st[, position := factor(unit_position, levels = c("N15", "E0", "P15"),
                        labels = c("in the cut", "edge", "in the forest"))]
ggplot(st, aes(position, lf_w)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.35, colour = "#1e8a5a", size = 1.2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5, colour = "#0b4f33", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ unit_forest_type) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = expression("Site latent variable " * w[i]))
```

Locations in aspen stands score higher than in spruce, and within a stand
type the forest side scores lowest; time since harvest pulls scores down as
the cut regrows. Together, position, forest type and years since harvest
explain `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * hab$r.squared)` of the variation in
$w_i$. None of those covariates was in the model: the site quantity was found
from the species. Its correlation with the number of visits is
`r fmt(r_vis_w)`, against `r fmt(r_vis_naive)` for the site score of the model
without detection, so it is a position on a habitat gradient rather than a
record of effort.

The species slopes from the quick fit to the `ever` table, the same model
without detection, correlate with these loadings at `r fmt(r_lam)`. For the
*direction* each species takes on the gradient, ignoring detection does little
harm here; for *how common* each species is, it does the damage shown above.
The reason is that detection which is the same everywhere for a species
scales that species' row of the table down, which moves its intercept a lot
and its pattern across sites less. Detection that changes along the gradient
(a bird easier to hear in open regrowth than in closed forest) would bias the
loadings as well, and these fits, with one $p_k$ per species, cannot see it.

## A sparse community: the Monongahela cameras

The camera table is the other extreme. Most species were photographed at a
handful of the 129 cameras, and per camera-day detection probabilities are
low, so most species carry almost no information about their own $\psi_k$ and
$p_k$.

```{r}
#| label: mono-load
fm <- cache$fits[["clipp_2024_monongahela_comm"]]
fm$conv
fm$comm_ms[, .(parameter = param, median = med, lower = lo, upper = hi, Rhat = rhat)]
mo <- as.data.table(fm$species)
mo[, `:=`(psi = plogis(ms_beta), psi_lo = plogis(ms_beta_lo), psi_hi = plogis(ms_beta_hi),
          np_psi = plogis(np_beta), p = plogis(ms_alpha))]
mo[, boundary := np_psi > 0.99 | is.na(np_beta_se) | np_beta_se > 10]
```

```{r}
#| label: mono-stats
#| echo: false
n_single <- sum(mo$n_sites_detected == 1)
n_bound <- sum(mo$boundary)
sing <- mo[n_sites_detected == 1]
```

`r n_single` of the `r nrow(mo)` species were detected at exactly one camera,
and `r n_bound` of the single-species fits end at the boundary or with a
standard error above 10 on the logit scale, typically "present at every
camera and almost never photographed". The community model gives each of
the single-camera species nearly the same answer, an occupancy around
`r fmt(median(sing$psi))` (median interval `r fmt(median(sing$psi_lo))` to
`r fmt(median(sing$psi_hi))`), about `r round(median(sing$psi) * fm$n_sites)` cameras in `r fm$n_sites` against the one at which
each was seen. That number is what the community distribution, and the low
per-day detection of the species that were seen often, say about a species
whose own data say almost nothing.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shrink-mono
#| fig-cap: "Occupancy with no pooling against occupancy under the community model, Monongahela cameras, with the community model's 95% credible intervals. Open points are single-species fits at the boundary. Hover for the species."
mo[, label := sprintf("%s\ndetected at %d cameras (%d camera-days)\nalone: psi %.2f%s\ncommunity: psi %.2f [%.2f, %.2f], p %.3f",
                      vernacularName, n_sites_detected, n_detections, np_psi,
                      ifelse(boundary, " (boundary)", ""), psi, psi_lo, psi_hi, p)]
g <- ggplot(mo, aes(psi, np_psi, text = label)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#c9ccc8") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = psi_lo, xmax = psi_hi), height = 0, colour = "#1e8a5a", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = boundary, size = n_sites_detected), shape = 21, colour = "#1e8a5a") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#1e8a5a", `TRUE` = "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7, guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Occupancy, community model (msPGOcc)", y = "Occupancy, each species alone (occu)")
plotly::ggplotly(g, tooltip = "text", width = 620, height = 560) |>
  plotly::config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

That is the honest reading of shrinkage. Treating species as draws from a
community turns an impossible single-species fit into a finite estimate, but
for a species seen once the estimate is mostly the community, and its
interval says so. The camera table also shows the price in computing. At
the default chain length both spOccupancy fits had parameters with
$\hat R$ above 1.1 and were rerun with chains five times as long (about
`r fmt(fm$conv$minutes[1], 1)` minutes each); the community model then
converges (largest $\hat R$ `r fmt(fm$conv$max_rhat[1])`), the latent-factor
model does not (`r fmt(fm$conv$max_rhat[2])`).

The site side is weaker still. In the model without detection the camera
variance is `r fmt(fm$rasch_var[["site"]], 3)` on the logit scale, against
`r fmt(fm$rasch_var[["species"]])` for species: with two species detected per
camera on average there is almost nothing from which to place a camera on a
gradient, and the latent-factor loadings (not shown) have intervals that span
zero for every species but the anchor, white-tailed deer. With this little
information per camera, the site side of the model is not estimable, and
only the species side is.

## What the correspondence buys, and where it stops

- **It is exact on the latent state.** The occupancy part of the
  latent-factor community model, $\text{logit}\,\psi_{ik} = \beta_k + \lambda_k w_i$ with
  $\beta_k$ drawn from a community normal, is a model with one latent quantity
  per site and random species parameters. With the same loading for every
  species it is the crossed random-effects model fit above to `ever`.
- **The standard community model has no site quantity.** The model of
  @dorazio2005, `msPGOcc()` here, has random species but treats sites as
  exchangeable apart from covariates. Saying "a community occupancy model is a
  model of sites and species" is true of the latent-factor version; for the
  standard one, the site side is whatever covariates are put on $\psi$.
- **Detection is an extra layer, and it is the one that matters for
  "how common".** Fitting the site-and-species model to the detections instead
  of the latent state estimates $\psi_k$ times the chance of detection, and
  ranks species partly by how detectable they are. A site score from the same
  fit is partly a record of effort.
- **The rest of the model carries over.** More than one latent variable is
  `n.factors > 1`. Species traits on $\beta_k$ (body mass, diet; see
  `eco_traits()`) explain why species differ instead of only how much. Site
  covariates on $\psi$ explain $w_i$ instead of discovering it.

The fits here are deliberately bare: intercept-only detection, no spatial
structure (the boreal locations come in transects of three, recorded in
`cluster_id`, and neighbouring locations share birds), and default priors.
Each is a line in the spOccupancy call.

## Reproducibility

Source: [`site/vignettes/species_items.qmd`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/species_items.qmd)
and [`species_items_compute.R`](https://github.com/ben-domingue/eco/blob/main/site/vignettes/species_items_compute.R)
in the eco repository. The spOccupancy and mirt fits were run on
`r cache$date_run` (3 chains of `r cache$mcmc$n.samples` iterations, `r cache$mcmc$n.burn`
burn-in, thinning `r cache$mcmc$n.thin`, rerun five times longer where any
$\hat R$ exceeded 1.1); the model without detection and the single-species
fits run live on this page. Data were read with `eco_set_version(12)`, so a
later release of the warehouse does not change the page.

```{r}
#| label: versions
#| echo: false
v <- eco_version()
cat(sprintf("eco version %s (Redivis eco %s, eco_meta %s, released %s)\n",
            v$eco_version, v$eco, v$eco_meta, substr(v$released, 1, 10)))
cat(sprintf("R %s; eco %s; lme4 %s; unmarked %s\n",
            getRversion(), packageVersion("eco"), packageVersion("lme4"), packageVersion("unmarked")))
cat("cached fits:", paste(names(cache$versions), cache$versions, collapse = "; "), "\n")
```
